advances: A necessary condition on every touching finite comparison in an open feasible chart; it gives no regularization of an arbitrary depth minimizer.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The cited comparison bounds actual depth above by $\max_i f_i(p)$, equals it at $p_0$, and already handles all nondeep sites by strict slack. Thus the maximum of the finitely many selected $C^2$ functions has a local minimum, and all selected functions have value $\beta$ at the base. The argument is identical if that upper comparison and slack are given directly.

Fix a common-kernel direction and write $q_i=D^2f_i(p_0)[\delta,\delta]$. The open chart contains $p_0+t\delta+t^2a/2$ for sufficiently small $t$ for each fixed acceleration $a$. Taylor expansion gives $f_i=\beta+(t^2/2)(g_i(a)+q_i)+o(t^2)$. If all second coefficients were negative, the maximum would decrease. Hence the affine space $q+\{(g_i(a))_i:a\text{ a chart vector}\}$ is disjoint from the open negative orthant. Separate the affine space on the larger side of a nonzero linear functional $\pi$. The orthant extends without bound in each negative coordinate, so all components of $\pi$ are nonnegative; its supremum there is zero. The affine space extends in both signs of each direction, so $\pi$ annihilates its direction space. Hence $\pi\cdot q\ge0$ and $\sum_i\pi_i g_i=0$. Normalize by its positive sum.

For one row the balance forces $g_1=0$ and then every direction qualifies. For two nonzero rows, the balance (for example with $\delta=0$) uses strictly positive coefficients and forces opposite proportionality; its only normalized weights are $c/(1+c),1/(1+c)$. On the common kernel these give the asserted quadratic form. In that case the functional $g_1-g_2=(1+c)g_1$ is nonzero, so one can choose $a$ with $(g_1-g_2)(a)=q_2-q_1$, equalizing the two second coefficients at their balanced average. When both rows vanish the probability maximum is simply $\max(q_1,q_2)$. With exactly one zero row all balancing weight lies on it. The upper bound uses one selected circuit at every globally deepest site; a first-order balance supported on a subset does not justify discarding the other sites from the comparison.
statement:
Use the finite-fiber touching deepest-circuit comparison of fact 1fa8cb387c27b040 on an open feasible chart. Suppose $p_0$ is a local minimum of actual maximal normalized depth with value $\beta$. At each old globally deepest site select any one available exact comparison whose ratio $f_i=\tau_{c_i}/M$ is $C^2$ near $p_0$. Put $g_i=Df_i(p_0)$. For every direction $\delta\in\bigcap_i\ker g_i$, there exist probabilities $\pi_i$ (possibly depending on $\delta$) such that
$$
\sum_i\pi_i g_i=0,\qquad \sum_i\pi_i D^2f_i(p_0)[\delta,\delta]\ge0.
$$
With one site $g_1=0$ and the selected Hessian is positive semidefinite. With two nonzero gradients one has $g_2=-c g_1$ for $c>0$, and $(cD^2f_1+D^2f_2)/(1+c)$ is nonnegative on $\ker g_1$. If both gradients vanish, the pointwise maximum of the two Hessian quadratic forms is nonnegative. If exactly one vanishes, its Hessian is nonnegative on the common kernel. These conclusions hold for every selection. The same necessary conditions apply if the touching comparison is supplied directly by actual nearby covers, with a persistent strict gap at the remaining sites.
title: Second-order necessary conditions for every selection of actual circuit covers
